# RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers

Yijun Li   Zhengxi Lu   Zhipiao Liu   Jinzheng Yu Affiliation: Zhejiang
University Affiliation: Huawei    Xutao Weng   Jian Shao   Yongliang
Shen Email: [{li_yijun, zhengxilu, syl}@zju.edu.cn ](mailto:)
Affiliation: Zhejiang University Affiliation: Huawei

###### Abstract

Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) extends RL with verifiable
rewards to open-ended tasks by scoring each response against
query-specific rubrics. Under group-relative optimization, however, a
rubric that every sampled response fails (unreachable) or passes
(saturated) gives all responses the same outcome and no learning signal;
in Qwen3-4B medical training, 60.88% of query–rubric observations are
inactive. We find that the two states lack different supervision:
stating an unreachable rubric in the prompt raises its satisfaction from
1.13% to 91.25%, whereas responses that all pass a saturated rubric
still differ in quality. We therefore propose RuACT (Rubrics as Adaptive
Critics and Teachers), which assigns each inactive rubric the role that
supplies what it lacks. Rubric as Teacher uses unreachable rubrics as
privileged information for reward-gated on-policy self-distillation, and
Rubric as Critic decomposes saturated rubrics into child rubrics that
separate current responses while sharing the parent’s weight. RuACT
outperforms GRPO, rubric reweighting, and rubric-guided exploration on
all four medical and scientific benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and achieves
the best average with Qwen3-1.7B. On initially unreachable rubrics,
unguided recovery rises from 35.02% to 42.86%, while child refinement
improves reward–quality alignment on independent rollouts from 57.74% to
60.77%. Code is available at
[https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/RuACT](https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/RuACT).

![Refer to caption](2611.09597v1/fig1-sculpture-vector-v17.png)

Figure 1: Inactive rubrics and RuACT. (a) Illustration of unreachable,
informative, and saturated rubrics and their distribution through
training. (b) How RuACT recovers inactive rubrics: reward-verified
guidance helps elicit missing behaviors, while finer-grained criticism
exposes details for further improvement.

## 1 Introduction

Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) extends the success of RL with
verifiable rewards (RLVR) in mathematics and code ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Cheng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib48)) to open-ended tasks, where response quality is
multidimensional and no single verifier suffices, by decomposing the
objective into fine-grained rubrics that each yield a reward ([Gunjal et
al., 2026](#bib.bib2); [Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib5); [Wei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6); [Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7); [Viswanathan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib31); [He et al., 2026](#bib.bib33)). Yet a task-relevant
rubric is not necessarily useful to the current policy: under
group-relative optimization, a rubric that no sampled response satisfies
(_unreachable_) or that every response satisfies (_saturated_) assigns
the same outcome to all rollouts and cancels out of the
advantage ([Tyagi et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)), leaving only rubrics with
intermediate pass rates _informative_. We refer to these two endpoint
states as _inactive rubrics_. Both are common: in Qwen3-4B medical
training, 25.19% of query–rubric pairs are unreachable and 35.69%
saturated
(Section [2](#S2 "2 Preliminary ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")).

Existing methods use rubrics as _critics_, prioritizing informative
feedback through reweighting and curricula ([Tyagi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18); [Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)), or continually
updating rubrics to sustain reward contrast ([Shao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib8); [Rezaei et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Ding et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20); [Xu et al., 2026d](#bib.bib39)). Yet reweighting and
curricula cannot restore within-group contrast for an inactive rubric,
because its constant contribution cancels under any weight
(Section [2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Rubric-Based GRPO ‣ 2 Preliminary ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"));
rubric updates may improve discrimination, but they replace the original
requirements rather than recover their supervision. Complementarily,
rubrics serve as _teachers_ by guiding exploration ([Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15); [Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib29)) or providing
privileged information for self-distillation ([Xia et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3); [Rezaei et al., 2026](#bib.bib27); [Gu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib28); [Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib43)). Such guidance can
elicit missing behaviors, but teaching existing requirements does not
itself sharpen their evaluation. Once a coarse requirement is satisfied,
further improvements may remain indistinguishable under its original
judgments.

The two endpoints, however, lack different kinds of supervision
(Section [2](#S2 "2 Preliminary ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")).
For an unreachable rubric, the behavior is missing from ordinary
rollouts: stating the rubric in the prompt raises the satisfaction rate
of a frozen Qwen3-4B from 1.13% to 91.25%. For a saturated rubric, the
distinction is missing: an independent fine-grained judge finds quality
differences among its responses in 71% of cases, compared with 29% for
unreachable rubrics. Teaching thus supplies behaviors but not contrast,
whereas finer evaluation supplies contrast where the behaviors already
exist. _Each inactive rubric should therefore take the role that
supplies what it lacks: a teacher when no response satisfies it, and a
finer-grained critic when every response does._

Following this principle, we propose RuACT (Rubrics as Adaptive Critics
and Teachers), which assigns each rubric a role by its current state in
each rollout group; informative rubrics keep their original rewards.
Rubric as Teacher appends unreachable rubrics to the prompt of a frozen
self-teacher and distills its token distributions on the best ordinary
rollout into the unguided policy. To avoid trading off other rubrics,
distillation is enabled only when a rubric-guided response outscores
every ordinary rollout. Rubric as Critic decomposes each saturated
rubric into child rubrics, retains those that separate current rollouts,
and lets them share the parent’s reward weight, which restores contrast
while preserving the original objective.

On four medical and scientific benchmarks, RuACT outperforms GRPO,
rubric reweighting, and rubric-guided exploration on every benchmark
with Qwen3-4B, with the largest gain on ResearchQA (from 64.82% under
GRPO to 69.44%), and achieves the best average with Qwen3-1.7B. Without
guidance, the trained policy satisfies 42.86% of initially unreachable
rubrics (35.02% under GRPO), and refined rewards agree better with an
independent judge (from 57.74% to 60.77%). The gains persist under a
second judge
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Policy-level Capability analysis ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")).

Our contributions are threefold:

- •
  We show that inactive rubrics cover 60.88% of query–rubric
  observations, and that unreachable rubrics lack behaviors while
  saturated rubrics lack distinctions among responses.
- •
  We propose RuACT, which assigns each inactive rubric the role that
  supplies its missing supervision: a teacher for unreachable rubrics
  and a critic for saturated ones.
- •
  Across two domains and two model scales, RuACT improves over strong
  rubric-based baselines, and analyses confirm that each role recovers
  the supervision it targets.

## 2 Preliminary

### 2.1 Rubric-Based GRPO

Given query $`x`$, GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)) samples $`G`$
responses $`\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$ from
$`\pi_{\theta_{\rm old}}(\cdot\mid x)`$ and evaluates them against
$`\mathcal{R}_{x}=\{(r_{j},w_{j})\}_{j=1}^{J_{x}}`$. Let
$`e_{ij}\in\{0,1\}`$ denote the judgment of response $`y_{i}`$ under
rubric $`r_{j}`$. With $`Z_{x}=\sum_{j:w_{j}>0}w_{j}`$, the reward and
advantage are

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
R_{i}=\frac{\sum_{j}w_{j}e_{ij}}{Z_{x}},\qquad A_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\overline{R}}{\sigma(R)+\epsilon},
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\overline{R}`$ and $`\sigma(R)`$ are the group reward mean and
standard deviation. When rubric $`r_{j}`$ receives identical judgments
across all $`G`$ responses, its contribution is constant and cancels
during reward centering; its weight still enters $`Z_{x}`$, but this
rescales $`R_{i}-\overline{R}`$ and $`\sigma(R)`$ alike. Reweighting, as
in our Reweight baseline, can therefore redistribute informative rubrics
but cannot create within-group contrast from an inactive one, up to
$`\epsilon`$.

### 2.2 Inactive Rubrics

For a rubric with nonzero weight, let $`s_{ij}=e_{ij}`$ if $`w_{j}>0`$
and $`s_{ij}=1-e_{ij}`$ otherwise, so $`s_{ij}=1`$ means $`y_{i}`$ meets
its intent. The satisfaction rate is

|     |                                                  |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widehat{p}_{j}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}s_{ij}.
       ```                                               |     | (2) |

As illustrated in
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")(a),
rubrics are *unreachable* when $`\widehat{p}_{j}=0`$, *informative* when
$`0<\widehat{p}_{j}<1`$, and *saturated* when $`\widehat{p}_{j}=1`$. The
endpoints are *inactive*, since their constant contributions cancel
(Section [2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Rubric-Based GRPO ‣ 2 Preliminary ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")).
Across 122,768 query–rubric observations during Qwen3-4B GRPO training
on RaR-Medicine, 25.19% are unreachable and 35.69% saturated, totaling
60.88% inactive observations. The fraction lies between 58.95% and
60.86% at each checkpoint shown in
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")(a).
Inactive rubrics are thus pervasive in rubric-based GRPO, and the two
states co-occur: 75.06% of query groups contain both unreachable and
saturated rubrics
(Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Rubric Inactivity across Training ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Training Analyses ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")),
so a single loop must handle both.

### 2.3 Rubrics as Teachers and Critics

We probe the two endpoints with inference-only diagnostics on
RaR-Medicine using the frozen Qwen3-4B base model. For each query, we
first sample $`G=8`$ ordinary responses and classify each query–rubric
pair as unreachable, informative, or saturated based on its binary
judgments.

Figure 2: Probes of inactive rubrics on frozen Qwen3-4B. (a) Fraction of
initially unreachable rubrics satisfied by at least one of $`K`$
independent ordinary samples; shading denotes 95% confidence intervals.
(b) Fraction of initially unreachable and saturated pairs whose
estimated quality variation $`V_{q}`$ exceeds $`v`$.

#### Rubrics as teachers.

Rubric guidance recovers most unreachable behaviors but adds no contrast
to saturated rubrics. More sampling recovers few: satisfying responses
appear for 17% and 21% of initially unreachable rubrics at $`K=32`$ and
$`64`$
(Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.3 Rubrics as Teachers and Critics ‣ 2 Preliminary ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")(a)).
In contrast, on 100 initially unreachable pairs, appending the target
rubric to the prompt raises satisfaction from 1.13% under fresh ordinary
prompting to 91.25%, versus 3.38% with generic instructions¹¹ 1 The
generic instructions are not length-matched.. The behavior is therefore
within the policy’s reach but rarely produced unprompted. For initially
saturated rubrics, the same intervention increases parent satisfaction
from 98.25% to 100.00%, and the judgments stay uniform.

#### Rubrics as critics.

Finer evaluation exposes quality differences that saturated judgments
hide. An independent judge scores each unchanged baseline response in
$`[0,1]`$ using only the query and parent rubric, without observing
binary verdicts, sibling responses, or children. For scores $`q_{i}`$,
we measure

|     |                                                       |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       V_{q}(x,j)=4\,\operatorname{Var}(q_{1},\ldots,q_{G}).
       ```                                                    |     | (3) |

Nonzero variation occurs in 71% of initially saturated rubrics, compared
with 29% of initially unreachable rubrics
(Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.3 Rubrics as Teachers and Critics ‣ 2 Preliminary ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")(b)).
Child rubrics turn this variation into reward contrast: children
selected on baseline responses and evaluated on fresh responses raise
the mean held-out contrast from 0.053 for the saturated parent to 0.365.
Children also add contrast for unreachable rubrics (from 0.036 to
0.230), but they can only reward partial progress already present in the
samples; the target behavior itself still has no positive example.
Independent quality scores remain LLM-based diagnostics rather than
expert ground truth.

#### Implications.

The two endpoints thus call for different roles. An unreachable rubric
should guide the policy toward a behavior it can produce but rarely
does, and the policy must learn it without seeing the rubric at
inference. A saturated rubric should be evaluated at a finer grain that
separates current responses, without changing how much it counts in the
reward.
Section [3](#S3 "3 Method ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
realizes these roles as Rubric as Teacher and Rubric as Critic.

## 3 Method

RuACT implements the two roles of
Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Rubrics as Teachers and Critics ‣ 2 Preliminary ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
and reassigns them in every rollout group as rubric states change
(Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Method ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")).
Unreachable rubrics guide a privileged self-teacher to provide
behavioral supervision, whereas saturated rubrics are expanded into more
discriminative evaluation items for reward construction. Informative
rubrics retain their original rewards. The two roles jointly optimize
the student policy by introducing a distillation loss and reshaping
group-relative advantages, respectively.

Figure 3: Rubrics as adaptive critics and teachers. Rollout judgments
identify unreachable ($`p=0`$), informative ($`0<p<1`$), and saturated
($`p=1`$) rubrics. As teachers, unreachable rubrics provide privileged
guidance, with reward-gated forward-KL supervision on prefixes of the
best ordinary rollout. As critics, saturated rubrics are expanded into
discriminative children sharing the parent weight budget. Original and
updated rubric rewards drive GRPO, while teacher supervision contributes
an auxiliary objective.

### 3.1 Rubric as Teacher

For unreachable rubrics, ordinary judgments provide no direct
within-group contrast. RuACT instead uses their requirements to
condition a frozen self-teacher, the rollout policy
$`\pi_{\theta_{\rm old}}`$, providing behavioral guidance beyond these
constant judgments ([Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)). For query
$`x`$, let $`\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$ be ordinary responses sampled from
$`\pi_{\theta_{\rm old}}(\cdot\mid x)`$. We select up to three
unreachable rubrics with the largest absolute weights and append them to
$`x`$, yielding a privileged prompt $`x^{+}`$.

Following the strategy of CriPO ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), we
select the highest-reward ordinary response to anchor teacher
supervision:

|     |                                                                |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       i^{*}=\arg\max_{1\leq i\leq G}R(y_{i}),\qquad y^{*}=y_{i^{*}}.
       ```                                                             |     | (4) |

Since privileged guidance may improve targeted behaviors at the expense
of other requirements ([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib12); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13); [Li et al., 2026c](#bib.bib45)), we introduce a
*reward-improvement gate* that accepts a rubric-guided response
$`\tilde{y}`$ sampled from $`x^{+}`$ by the frozen policy only if its
overall reward exceeds that of every ordinary rollout:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{x}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[R(\widetilde{y})>\max_{1\leq i\leq G}R(y_{i})\right].
``` |  | (5) |

The guided response only gates distillation; supervision stays on the
student’s own text. For groups passing the reward-improvement gate,
teacher and student are evaluated on identical prefixes of $`y^{*}`$ but
receive different prompt information. At each supervised position $`t`$,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle q_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{stopgrad}\!\left[\pi_{\theta_{\rm old}}(\cdot\mid x^{+},y^{*}_{<t})\right],`$ |  | (6) |
|  | $`\displaystyle p_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y^{*}_{<t}).`$ |  |  |

Only the teacher observes the target rubrics. The ordinary policy
receives token-level supervision through forward KL ([Agarwal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22); [Pan et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell_{\rm Distillation}(x)=\frac{a_{x}}{|M_{x}|}\sum_{t\in M_{x}}D_{\rm KL}(q_{t}\|p_{t}),
``` |  | (7) |

where $`M_{x}`$ contains the valid supervised positions. This encourages
the student to follow rubric-conditioned guidance without requiring
rubric input at inference. Further implementation details and the
privileged teacher prompt are provided in
Appendices [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 RuACT Implementation ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Settings ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
and [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Privileged Teacher Prompt ‣ Appendix E Prompt Templates ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
respectively.

### 3.2 Rubric as Critic

For saturated rubrics, uniform success judgments eliminate within-group
reward contrast, potentially masking finer-grained differences in
response quality. RuACT adapts their critic role by evaluating finer
aspects of the parent requirement, enabling finer-grained distinctions
among responses that receive identical parent-level rewards ([Fan et
al., 2024](#bib.bib35); [Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)).

For a selected saturated parent rubric $`r_{j}`$, a proposal model
initially generates candidate child rubrics using only the query and
parent description, without observing rollout responses. We evaluate the
candidates on current rollouts to identify those that restore
within-group reward contrast. Let $`e_{ijk}\in\{0,1\}`$ denote the
judgment of response $`i`$ under candidate child $`k`$. Eligible
children must have non-endpoint pass rates:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_{j}=\left\{k:0<\sum_{i=1}^{G}e_{ijk}<G\right\}.
``` |  | (8) |

When too few candidates qualify, their judgment feedback guides an
additional proposal round. We retain at most three eligible children per
parent, forming $`\mathcal{K}_{j}\subseteq\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_{j}`$,
for reward discrimination.

The parent and its retained children share the original reward weight
budget. For $`m_{j}=|\mathcal{K}_{j}|>0`$, their combined contribution
is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R^{\prime}_{ij}=\frac{w_{j}}{Z_{x}}\left[(1-\lambda)e_{ij}+\frac{\lambda}{m_{j}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{j}}e_{ijk}\right].
``` |  | (9) |

Here $`0<\lambda\leq 1`$ controls the weight allocated to children.
While the parent may remain saturated, its children can introduce
additional reward contrast without increasing the family’s weight
budget. If no valid child is found, the parent contribution is
preserved. We use $`\lambda=0.50`$. Further implementation details and
child-rubric proposal prompts are provided in
Appendices [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 RuACT Implementation ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Settings ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
and [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Child Rubric Generation and Regeneration ‣ Appendix E Prompt Templates ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
respectively.

### 3.3 Joint Optimization

The critic determines the rubric rewards used to compute group-relative
advantages, while the teacher provides an auxiliary token-level
objective ([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib44)). For a batch $`\mathcal{B}`$
containing $`Q`$ query groups, RuACT optimizes

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RuACT}}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\rm GRPO}(\theta;R^{\prime})\!+\!\frac{\beta}{Q}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{B}}\ell_{\rm Distill}(x),
``` |  | (10) |

where $`R^{\prime}`$ combines unchanged rubric rewards with updated
parent-family contributions. Groups rejected by the teacher gate
contribute zero auxiliary loss but remain in GRPO, including any valid
critic-side reward updates. We use $`\beta=0.1`$ for Qwen3-1.7B and
$`\beta=0.05`$ for Qwen3-4B.

### 4.1 Setup

#### Datasets and Evaluation.

We evaluate RuACT on both medical and scientific reasoning. RaR-Medicine
and RaR-Science ([Gunjal et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) serve as the training
datasets and in-domain evaluation benchmarks for the two domains,
respectively. For out-of-domain evaluation, we use HealthBench ([Arora
et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)) for medicine and ResearchQA ([Yifei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)) for science. We conduct experiments with Qwen3-1.7B
and Qwen3-4B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib24)) using a verl-based
implementation ([Sheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)). All methods are
trained for 200 optimization steps under matched budgets, using
Qwen3-32B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib24)) as the rubric judge during
training and Deepseek-v4.1-flash ([Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib14)) as the
evaluation judge. Further details on datasets, training configurations,
and evaluation protocols are provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Detailed Experimental Settings ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
and
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Policy-level Capability analysis ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
re-evaluates all models with a second judge.

#### Baselines and Models.

We compare RuACT against representative baselines covering different
optimization strategies. GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)) provides
standard group-relative optimization, while OPSD ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)) introduces privileged-information-guided
distillation. For rubric-based methods, RuscaRL ([Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15)) represents *rubrics as teachers*, guiding policy
exploration through rubric-based scaffolding. In contrast, Reweight, our
implementation inspired by POW3R ([Tyagi et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)),
represents *rubrics as critics*, adaptively weighting rubrics based on
their current informativeness. We additionally evaluate RuACT-Teacher
and RuACT-Critic to isolate the contributions of recovering unreachable
and saturated rubrics, respectively, and compare with DAPO-style
sampling and GRPO+OPSD in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers").
All locally implemented methods share the same training and evaluation
protocol
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Detailed Experimental Settings ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")),
while OPSD results are quoted from CriPO ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib3))
with another judge.

### 4.2 Main Results

#### Overall Performance.

As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
RuACT achieves the best average at both scales, raising GRPO from 45.04%
to 47.17% on Qwen3-1.7B and from 56.52% to 59.12% on Qwen3-4B, and
exceeding the strongest local baseline (RuscaRL at 45.78% and Reweight
at 57.28%, respectively). At 4B, RuACT is best on all four benchmarks,
with the largest gains on the out-of-domain HealthBench (from 37.62% to
40.12%) and ResearchQA (from 64.82% to 69.44%). At 1.7B, the single-role
variants already lead on individual benchmarks, and combining them
mainly improves the average. Both single-role variants outperform GRPO
on average at both scales, so each role contributes independently.
Although trained only on medical questions, RuACT also improves over the
base model on MT-Bench and FollowBench
(Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Comparison with Alternative Optimization Strategies. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")).

Figure 4: Recovery of initially unreachable rubrics (Qwen3-4B,
RaR-Medicine). A rubric is recovered if any of eight unguided rollouts
satisfies it. (a) During training. (b) Grouped by whether rubric
guidance elicits the behavior from the base model.

### 4.3 Analysis

#### Unreachable Does Not Mean Unlearnable.

Rubrics unreachable under the current policy can become learnable
through targeted teacher supervision. We track 931 initially unreachable
rubrics from 331 fixed RaR-Medicine training queries, measuring recovery
every 40 steps using eight unguided rollouts. As shown in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Overall Performance. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
RuACT-Teacher alone raises the recovery rate at step 200 from 35.02%
under GRPO to 38.78%, and the full method reaches 42.86%. Because
recovery is measured without privileged prompts, these gains reflect the
policy’s own generation.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Overall Performance. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")(b)
shows that RuACT achieves larger average recovery gains on initially
rubric-elicitable behaviors (+5.5 pp) than on those not elicited (+1.1
pp).

|----|----|----|
|  parent rubric-only    |  57.74    |  65.92 |
|  w/ Decomposed    |  60.77    |  88.85 |
|  w/ Shuffled Decomposed    |  53.62    |  90.44 |

Table 2: Quality alignment of refined rewards. Reward-quality alignment
and coverage.

Figure 5: Reward discrimination on independent rollouts. Within-group
reward STD with and without child-rubric refinement for (a) RuACT-Critic
and (b) RuACT on Qwen3-4B RaR-Medicine. Rollouts are sampled
independently of those used for child selection.

#### Saturated Does Not Mean Indistinguishable.

We evaluate child refinement on fresh rollouts, separate from those used
for selection. Refinement raises within-group reward STD by 11.34% for
RuACT-Critic and 10.02% for RuACT
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Unreachable Does Not Mean Unlearnable. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")).

We further assess whether this additional contrast reflects response
quality using blind judgments on 300 rollout groups (2,400 responses).
We measure reward coverage as the fraction of response pairs assigned
different rewards, and quality alignment as the agreement between reward
rankings and independent quality judgments, excluding judge ties and
assigning half credit to reward ties. Both metrics are averaged within
groups and then across groups.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Unreachable Does Not Mean Unlearnable. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
shows that matched children improve quality alignment from 57.74% to
60.77% and reward coverage from 65.92% to 88.85%. Shuffled children
achieve higher coverage (90.44%) but lower alignment (53.62%),
indicating that reward discrimination alone does not guarantee alignment
with response quality.

#### Joint Improvements across Inactive Rubrics.

We examine how the teacher and critic roles jointly improve policy
behavior.
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Saturated Does Not Mean Indistinguishable. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
compares unreachable-rate reduction and child-rubric satisfaction gains
relative to GRPO. RuACT-Teacher achieves a larger unreachable reduction
than RuACT-Critic (+1.58 vs. +1.32 pp), while RuACT-Critic yields
greater fine-grained satisfaction gains (+3.16 vs. +1.81 pp). RuACT
achieves the largest unreachable reduction (+1.93 pp) while maintaining
substantial child-rubric satisfaction gains (+2.73 pp). These results
show the distinct contributions of both roles and their joint benefits.

#### Comparison with Alternative Optimization Strategies.

We further compare RuACT with dynamic sampling and
privileged-information distillation strategies. As shown in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Saturated Does Not Mean Indistinguishable. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
RuACT achieves the highest average among locally evaluated methods
(48.23%), above DAPO-style sampling (47.78%) and GRPO+OPSD (47.11%).
DAPO-style sampling nearly matches RuACT on RaR-Medicine (56.29% vs.
56.34%) but trails on HealthBench (39.27% vs. 40.12%). The two act at
different levels: dynamic sampling discards groups whose total rewards
are constant, whereas RuACT recovers individual rubrics inside groups
whose total rewards still vary, so they can be combined.

#### General Capability Preservation

We further examine whether medicine-specific training compromises
general instruction-following capabilities. Using the
RaR-Medicine-trained checkpoints, we evaluate Base and RuACT on MT-Bench
and FollowBench with Qwen3-Max as the judge. As shown in
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Comparison with Alternative Optimization Strategies. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
RuACT improves both MT-Bench turns and FollowBench success rates at both
model scales. These results suggest that recovering inactive supervision
preserves the evaluated general capabilities while improving
domain-specific performance.

## 5 Ablation Study

|                   |          |             |       |
|-------------------|----------|-------------|-------|
|  Variant          | RaR-Med. | HealthBench | Avg.  |
|  RuACT            | 56.34    | 40.12       | 48.23 |
| Rubric as Teacher |          |             |       |
|  RuACT-Teacher    | 55.15    | 38.57       | 46.86 |
|    w/o Gate       | 55.18    | 37.45       | 46.32 |
| Rubric as Critic  |          |             |       |
|  RuACT-Critic     | 55.50    | 38.77       | 47.14 |
|    w/o Filter     | 54.99    | 38.50       | 46.75 |

Table 5: Ablation study of RuACT on Qwen3-4B. Scores are reported in %
on RaR-Medicine and HealthBench, with Avg. denoting their unweighted
mean.

#### Both Recovery Roles Matter.

Neither teacher guidance nor critic refinement alone matches the full
RuACT framework. As shown in
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5 Ablation Study ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
RuACT achieves an average of 48.23%, compared with 46.86% for
RuACT-Teacher and 47.14% for RuACT-Critic. This supports the distinct
contributions of recovering unreachable behaviors and restoring reward
discrimination.

#### Teacher Guidance Must Be Selective.

Rubric-conditioned guidance does not always yield better overall
responses. Across 10,780 gate evaluations in full RuACT training, only
44.86% of guided candidates exceed the best student rollout in aggregate
rubric reward, and the acceptance rate decreases from 50.69% in the
first 50 steps to 42.61% in the last 50 steps, suggesting fewer
opportunities for reward-improving guidance later in training. Removing
the gate leaves RaR-Medicine nearly unchanged (55.15% vs. 55.18%) but
reduces HealthBench from 38.57% to 37.45%, lowering the average from
46.86% to 46.32%. The gate thus blocks guided responses that improve the
target rubrics at the expense of others.

#### Effective Refinement Requires Filtering.

Generating child rubrics does not guarantee informative reward
distinctions. Among 93,523 judged child candidates, 64.10% receive
uniform judgments across all eight rollouts, while only 21.06% are
ultimately retained after filtering and selection limits. This limits
unnecessary reward modifications from candidates without within-group
contrast. Moreover, the proportion of fully satisfied candidates
increases from 43.49% to 54.00% across training, highlighting the
continued need for filtering. Removing the filter reduces the average
from 47.14% to 46.75%, indicating that only children that separate
current responses are useful.

## 6 Related Work

#### Rubrics as rewards and critics.

Rubric-based RL aggregates judgments on checkable criteria into
rewards ([Gunjal et al., 2026](#bib.bib2); [Huang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5); [Viswanathan et al., 2026](#bib.bib31); [Jacob Dineen
et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [He et al., 2026](#bib.bib33)), using
expert-written or LLM-synthesized rubrics ([Li et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib7); [Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib34); [Shen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib36)). Adaptive critics
reweight or schedule rubrics ([Tyagi et al., 2026](#bib.bib18); [Chen et
al., 2026](#bib.bib19)), reshape how judgments become rewards ([Xu et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib37); [Lan et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Xu et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib41); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib42)), or evolve
rubrics with the policy ([Shao et al., 2025](#bib.bib8); [Rezaei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9); [Ding et al., 2026](#bib.bib20); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib21); [Sheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib38); [Xu et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib39)). Reweighting cannot fix a constant rubric, and
evolving methods revise the whole rubric set; RuACT refines only
saturated rubrics within their weight.

#### Rubrics as teachers.

Rubrics also guide generation through scaffolded exploration or
hindsight replay ([Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib15); [Zhang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib29)), or serve as privileged context distilled into the
policy ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [Hübotter et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23); [Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib43); [Rezaei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib27); [Gu et al., 2026](#bib.bib28); [Pan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46)), or combined with group-relative updates ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib44); [Han et al., 2026](#bib.bib17); [Lu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30)). Distillation supplies dense token-level
supervision ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)), but privileged
teachers may also transfer undesirable behaviors ([Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Li et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib45)), so guidance should be verified before distillation.
Closest to ours, CriPO injects unmet criteria into a teacher anchored on
the best student response and corrects advantages for suppressed
criteria ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). These methods cover only the
failing side. RuACT teaches only rubrics all rollouts fail, reward-gates
the guidance, and adds a critic for saturated ones. Unlike direct
imitation of guided responses, RuACT distills rubric-conditioned
distributions on prefixes of ordinary student rollouts.

## 7 Conclusion

Rubric inactivity does not necessarily imply a lack of learning value.
We introduce RuACT, which adaptively uses rubrics as teachers and
critics to recover supervision lost under the current policy. For
unreachable rubrics, reward-gated teacher guidance helps the policy
acquire previously unmet behaviors; for saturated rubrics, critic
refinement restores fine-grained reward discrimination. Across medical
and scientific reasoning benchmarks, RuACT achieves the highest average
performance at both model scales. Analyses show improved unguided
recovery of unreachable rubrics and more quality-aligned reward signals
from refined rubrics. These findings highlight the value of recovering
behavioral and evaluative supervision.

## Limitations

RuACT relies on LLM-based rubric judgments and child-rubric proposals.
Although our experiments evaluate reward–quality alignment using an
independent judge, the generated children may not always faithfully
capture the intended requirements. Improving the reliability of rubric
refinement remains a direction for future work.

Rubric states are identified from a limited group of $`G=8`$ responses.
Consequently, unreachable and saturated labels reflect the current
samples rather than intrinsic properties of the policy. Larger or
adaptive groups could improve state estimation, especially for rarely
satisfied rubrics.

Our experiments primarily cover medicine and science with Qwen3-1.7B and
Qwen3-4B. Generalization to larger models and broader domains remains to
be explored. Moreover, teacher guidance and critic refinement require
additional inference during training, which future work could reduce.

## Ethical Statement

Our models are trained and evaluated on medical and scientific question
answering. All evaluations rely on LLM judges rather than expert review,
and the trained models are research artifacts that should not be used
for clinical advice or decisions without professional oversight.
Rubric-guided distillation may also propagate biases present in the
rubrics or judges. We use public datasets and models.

## Appendix A Detailed Experimental Settings

### A.1 Datasets

We train on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science ([Gunjal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)) and evaluate on their test splits, HealthBench ([Arora
et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)), and ResearchQA ([Yifei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)).
Table [6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ A.1 Datasets ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Settings ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
reports the sizes of the prepared inputs. HealthBench and ResearchQA
each use a fixed 500-example subset for evaluation only. The HealthBench
subset is sampled with seed 42. All methods evaluated in our experiments
use the same frozen evaluation inputs and rubric weights.

| Dataset      | Train  | Evaluation |
|--------------|--------|------------|
| RaR-Medicine | 17,926 | 2,242      |
| RaR-Science  | 18,302 | 2,292      |
| HealthBench  | –      | 500        |
| ResearchQA   | –      | 500        |

Table 6: Dataset sizes used in our experiments. Counts refer to examples
in the prepared splits. HealthBench and ResearchQA are evaluation
subsets.

### A.2 Training Setup

Policies are initialized from Qwen3-1.7B or Qwen3-4B and trained with
verl, BF16 FSDP, vLLM, and AdamW on two NVIDIA A800 GPUs.
Table [7](#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ A.2 Training Setup ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Settings ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
gives the shared optimization settings and the standard RaR-Medicine
sequence limits. Methods use the same initialization, training data,
seed, query batch size, and rollout group size unless a difference is
specified below. We match the number of training steps. Teacher guidance
and rubric generation incur additional inference cost.

|  Hyperparameter              | Value        |
|------------------------------|--------------|
|  Training steps              | 200          |
|  Queries per batch           | 64           |
|  Responses per query, $`G`$  | 8            |
|  PPO mini-batch size         | 32           |
|  PPO epochs per batch        | 1            |
|  Learning rate               | $`10^{-6}`$  |
|  Learning-rate warmup steps  | 12           |
|  Reference KL coefficient    | $`10^{-3}`$  |
|  Rollout temperature         | 1.0          |
|  Rollout top-$`p`$           | 1.0          |
|  Maximum prompt length       | 1,024 tokens |
|  Maximum response length     | 4,096 tokens |
|  Maximum context length      | 6,144 tokens |

Table 7: Policy-training settings. Sequence limits are for the standard
RaR-Medicine configuration.

We use seed 42, disable thinking and top-$`k`$ filtering, and save
checkpoints every 20 steps. The actor micro-batch size is one per GPU,
except for Reweight and RuscaRL, which use four. Dynamic sampling is
enabled only in the DAPO-style baseline.

### A.3 Baseline Implementations

#### GRPO.

GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)) optimizes the original rubric
reward without teacher guidance or child-rubric refinement.

#### Reweight.

We implement a group-based reweighting control inspired by POW3R ([Tyagi
et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)). It recomputes weights from the current
response group, without maintaining a historical weighting state. Let
$`g_{ij}`$ denote binary satisfaction after polarity adjustment: for a
negative-weight criterion, $`g_{ij}`$ is one minus its raw satisfaction
verdict. For responses with valid judgments, indexed by
$`\mathcal{G}_{j}`$, we compute

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\widehat{p}_{j}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}_{j}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{G}_{j}}g_{ij},`$ |  | (11) |
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{j}`$ | $`\displaystyle=1+4\eta\widehat{p}_{j}(1-\widehat{p}_{j}),`$ |  |  |

where $`\eta=0.5`$. With $`\widetilde{w}_{j}=|w_{j}|a_{j}`$, the
response reward is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{i}^{\mathrm{reweight}}=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}}\widetilde{w}_{j}g_{ij}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}}\widetilde{w}_{j}},
``` |  | (12) |

where $`\mathcal{J}_{i}`$ contains valid judgments for response $`i`$.
Missing verdicts are excluded. Uniformly passed or failed criteria
retain their original weight magnitude. This baseline implements the
variance-based reweighting idea rather than the full POW3R algorithm.

#### RuscaRL.

Our RuscaRL ([Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)) implementation generates
rubric-guided responses and uses the vanilla policy loss. The Qwen3-4B
RaR-Science run uses prompt and context limits of 8,192 and 12,288
tokens, respectively, with vLLM memory utilization set to 0.50.

#### GRPO+OPSD.

This baseline augments GRPO with distillation from a teacher conditioned
on the complete rubric. It does not use unreachable-rubric selection or
critic refinement. Our gated variant accepts guidance using the original
rubric reward and uses an ordinary rollout for distillation. For
Qwen3-4B, the effective teacher coefficient is 0.05 with a 50-step
warmup.

#### DAPO-style Sampling.

This baseline adds bounded dynamic sampling to the GRPO objective. Other
components of DAPO are not included.

### A.4 RuACT Implementation

Table [8](#A1.T8 "Table 8 ‣ A.4 RuACT Implementation ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Settings ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
lists the teacher and critic settings. The objectives and
child-eligibility rule are defined in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Method ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers");
prompts are provided in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Prompt Templates ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers").

|                                       |             |
|---------------------------------------|-------------|
|  Hyperparameter                       | Setting     |
| Teacher                               |             |
|  Target rubrics per query             | 3           |
|  Guided responses per selected query  | 1           |
|  Effective $`\beta`$ (1.7B / 4B)      | 0.10 / 0.05 |
|  Coefficient warmup steps             | 50          |
| Critic                                |             |
|  Selected parents per query           | 3           |
|  Initial candidates per parent        | 5           |
|  Additional proposal rounds (max.)    | 1           |
|  Retained children per parent         | 3           |
|  Active children per query            | 3           |
|  Parent–child mixture, $`\lambda`$    | 0.50        |

Table 8: RuACT hyperparameters. Critic settings describe the Qwen3-4B
RaR-Medicine configuration. Selection and retention counts are maxima.

#### Teacher.

We select unreachable rubrics by descending absolute weight and generate
one guided response per selected query. The full original-rubric reward
determines gate acceptance. For accepted groups, distillation uses the
highest-reward valid ordinary rollout as its trajectory, with the
teacher and student conditioned on the same response prefix. Only the
teacher receives the privileged rubric instructions. Rejected groups
retain the GRPO update. Forward KL uses the top-64 vocabulary entries
and a residual bin. The reported $`\beta`$ is the effective coefficient,
equal to the internal loss coefficient multiplied by $`G=8`$.

#### Critic.

Candidates are proposed from the query and parent description. Rollout
texts are used for validation and selection, not proposal generation. If
too few candidates pass, one further proposal round uses feedback on
rejected candidates. Up to three children are retained per selected
parent, while at most three children per query enter the active reward
view. Thus, in
Eq. [9](#S3.E9 "In 3.2 Rubric as Critic ‣ 3 Method ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
$`m_{j}`$ counts the active children of parent $`j`$. A parent with no
active child keeps its original contribution. Original GRPO rubrics are
not subject to the child cap.

### A.5 Evaluation and Judges

Qwen3-32B supplies binary judgments during training, including
child-rubric validation. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B generates child-rubric
proposals. We use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for the main benchmark evaluation
and Qwen3.7-Max for the judge-robustness evaluation.

For each evaluation query, we generate one response with temperature
0.70, top-$`p`$ 0.80, seed 42, and a 4,096-token response limit.
Thinking and top-$`k`$ filtering are disabled. The same frozen responses
are used across evaluation judges. RaR scores use binary judgments and
the explicit signed rubric weights. HealthBench divides signed rubric
points by the total positive weight. Aggregation is fixed across methods
within each benchmark.

OPSD^(∗) scores quoted from CriPO ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)) are
external reference results. CriPO uses filtered RaR splits and a
different evaluation judge, so these scores are reported separately from
our matched comparisons.

## Appendix B Supplementary Training Analyses

### B.1 Rubric Inactivity across Training

Figure 7: Rubric inactivity persists and co-occurs throughout GRPO
training. (a) Query-group composition by unreachable (U) and saturated
(S) rubric occurrence across five 40-step phases. (b) Mean number of U
or S rubrics per affected group, conditional on at least one occurrence.
Statistics use the original rubrics and eight rollouts per query group
from Qwen3-4B training on RaR-Medicine.

#### Both Forms of Inactivity Persist and Co-occur.

We examine rubric inactivity across all 200 steps of Qwen3-4B GRPO
training on RaR-Medicine, comprising 12,800 query–step groups and
122,768 original query–rubric observations. We classify each original
rubric as unreachable, informative, or saturated based on the binary
judgments of eight rollouts, and divide training into five 40-step
intervals. For each group, we measure the occurrence of each inactive
state and its conditional rubric count, averaged only over groups
containing that state.

As shown in
Figure [7](#A2.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ B.1 Rubric Inactivity across Training ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Training Analyses ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")(a),
99.06% of query groups contain at least one inactive rubric, and 75.06%
contain *both* unreachable and saturated rubrics. The co-occurrence rate
remains high across all five phases (73.52–76.41%). Unreachable-rubric
occurrence remains near 84%, whereas saturated-rubric occurrence rises
from 88.75% to 91.48%.
Figure [7](#A2.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ B.1 Rubric Inactivity across Training ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Training Analyses ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")(b)
further shows that affected groups contain an average of 2.88
unreachable or 3.79 saturated rubrics over training. These findings show
that the two inactive states are widespread and frequently coexist
within the same rollout group, motivating RuACT’s state-dependent use of
rubrics as teachers and critics within a shared training loop.

### B.2 Training Dynamics

#### RuACT Sustains Higher Policy Entropy.

Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ RuACT Sustains Higher Policy Entropy. ‣ B.2 Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Training Analyses ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
[9](#A2.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ RuACT Sustains Higher Policy Entropy. ‣ B.2 Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Training Analyses ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers"),
[10](#A2.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ RuACT Sustains Higher Policy Entropy. ‣ B.2 Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Training Analyses ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")
compares the training dynamics of GRPO, RuACT-Teacher, RuACT-Critic, and
RuACT on Qwen3-4B RaR-Medicine. While policy entropy declines across all
methods, RuACT maintains substantially higher entropy throughout most of
training. RuACT-Teacher also exhibits slower entropy decay than GRPO,
whereas RuACT-Critic follows a trajectory closer to standard GRPO.
Meanwhile, RuACT produces consistently longer responses as training
progresses, suggesting more sustained behavioral exploration under
recovered supervision. However, greater entropy and response length do
not necessarily imply higher response quality. The reward curves also
exhibit different magnitudes and fluctuations, but their absolute values
are not directly comparable, since RuACT and RuACT-Critic incorporate
refined child-rubric rewards while GRPO and RuACT-Teacher retain the
original reward formulation.

Figure 8: Training reward on Qwen3-4B RaR-Medicine. Reward magnitudes
are not directly comparable across different scoring rules.

### C.2 Policy-Level Capability Analysis

We provide additional details on the capability analysis in
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Saturated Does Not Mean Indistinguishable. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers").
The evaluation uses Qwen3-4B checkpoints on RaR-Medicine, with $`G=8`$
unguided responses sampled per query for each method. Both axes measure
percentage-point improvements relative to GRPO, using fixed evaluation
inputs and consistent rubric judgments.

#### Unreachable-Rate Reduction.

The horizontal axis measures the reduction in unreachable rubrics over
the full test set, comprising 21,500 query–rubric pairs. For method
$`m`$, let $`s^{(m)}_{xij}\in\{0,1\}`$ denote whether response $`i`$
satisfies original rubric $`j`$. We compute

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle U_{m}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{(x,j)\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{I}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{G}s^{(m)}_{xij}=0\right],`$ |  | (13) |
|  | $`\displaystyle X_{m}`$ | $`\displaystyle=U_{\mathrm{GRPO}}-U_{m},`$ |  |  |

where $`\mathcal{T}`$ denotes all test query–rubric pairs. Thus, this
metric measures the overall reduction in unreachable incidence, rather
than recovery on a fixed initially unreachable cohort.

#### Child-Rubric Satisfaction Gain.

The vertical axis evaluates finer-grained satisfaction on a fixed cohort
$`\mathcal{S}`$ of 1,954 parent rubrics identified as saturated under
the Base model. Child rubrics are generated using a fixed Qwen3.6
proposal model and shared across all evaluated methods. Let
$`\mathcal{C}_{xj}`$ denote the shared children of parent $`(x,j)`$, and
let $`c^{(m)}_{xijk}`$ be the binary satisfaction judgment for child
$`k`$. We define

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle C_{m}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{(x,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{1}{G|\mathcal{C}_{xj}|}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{C}_{xj}}c^{(m)}_{xijk},`$ |  | (14) |
|  | $`\displaystyle Y_{m}`$ | $`\displaystyle=C_{m}-C_{\mathrm{GRPO}}.`$ |  |  |

Using the same parents and children ensures that all methods are
evaluated against identical fine-grained requirements. Unlike reward
discrimination, this metric measures the policy’s satisfaction of these
requirements, rather than the variance of its training rewards.

## Appendix E Prompt Templates

We provide the prompt templates used for rubric-conditioned teacher
guidance, child-rubric proposal, and binary rubric evaluation. Runtime
inputs are denoted by braced placeholders. The templates cover the
positive-only and mixed-polarity teacher instructions, the initial and
feedback-guided child-rubric proposal rounds, and the shared binary
judgment format.

### E.1 Privileged Teacher Prompt

For currently unreachable rubrics of either polarity, the teacher
receives the original query and privileged feedback specifying up to
three unmet requirements or penalized behaviors, ranked by absolute
rubric weight. Positive-weight rubrics are expressed as \[REQUIRE\]
instructions, and negative-weight rubrics as \[AVOID\] instructions. The
rubric-guided response is used only for the overall-reward acceptance
gate. For accepted groups, teacher–student forward KL is evaluated on
identical prefixes of the highest-reward ordinary rollout, rather than
by directly imitating the guided response
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Rubric as Teacher ‣ 3 Method ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers")).

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

{original user prompt}

Private rubric feedback: every sampled answer failed the positive
requirements below. Satisfy them while preserving correct content. Do
not mention this feedback in the answer.

1. \[REQUIRE\] {failed positive rubric description}

2. \[REQUIRE\] {another failed positive rubric description}

…

#### Polarity-aware guidance.

The prompt is chosen according to the selected unreachable rubrics. When
all selected rubrics have positive weights, the positive-only template
above is used. When at least one negative-weight rubric is selected, the
following mixed-polarity template is used instead. Only the selected
\[REQUIRE\] and \[AVOID\] instructions are included.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

{original user prompt}

Private rubric feedback: every sampled answer failed the required points
below or committed the listed pitfalls. Satisfy every \[REQUIRE\] point
and do not commit any \[AVOID\] pitfall, while preserving correct
content. Do not mention this feedback in the answer.

1. \[REQUIRE\] {failed positive rubric description}

2. \[AVOID\] {failed negative-weight pitfall description}

…

### E.2 Child Rubric Generation and Regeneration

For a saturated parent rubric, child candidates are obtained from a
preverified library when available and supplemented by a proposal model
conditioned on the query, parent title and description, and fixed
few-shot demonstrations. The initial proposal does not observe current
rollout responses or their judgments. Candidates must remain within the
parent’s objective and be independently judgeable against a single
answer. If too few candidates pass judgment-based selection, at most one
additional proposal round is performed using feedback on rejected
candidates, without revealing any rollout response text. The
demonstrations below are included through the corresponding runtime
placeholder.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Few-shot demonstrations (format and specificity only; do not copy their
medical content):

Example 1

Query: A patient has acute chest pain. What is the initial evaluation?

Parent rubric: Identifies time-sensitive evaluation for life-threatening
cardiac causes.

Valid output:

{"candidates":\[

{"title":"Serial ischemia testing","completion_point":"States that
serial ECG and troponin assessment are needed when acute coronary
syndrome remains a concern."},

{"title":"Immediate instability check","completion_point":"Checks for
hemodynamic instability before proceeding with routine evaluation."}

\]}

Example 2

Query: How should suspected bacterial meningitis be managed initially?

Parent rubric: Recommends prompt empiric treatment for suspected
bacterial meningitis.

Valid output:

{"candidates":\[

{"title":"Do not delay treatment","completion_point":"States that
empiric antibiotics should not be delayed when lumbar puncture or
imaging would postpone treatment."},

{"title":"Blood cultures first when
feasible","completion_point":"Requests blood cultures before antibiotics
when this can be done without delaying treatment."}

\]}

Example 3

Query: What discharge advice is appropriate after a new medication is
started?

Parent rubric: Provides safe, actionable follow-up advice.

Valid output:

{"candidates":\[

{"title":"Specific warning signs","completion_point":"Names concrete
symptoms that require urgent reassessment rather than giving only
generic follow-up advice."},

{"title":"Defined follow-up timing","completion_point":"Specifies when
and with whom the patient should follow up."}

\]}

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are refining one rubric for a RaR training example.

{few-shot demonstrations above}

Now solve the target example. Follow the demonstrated JSON shape, but
derive every completion point only from the target query and parent
rubric.

User query:

{query}

Parent rubric:

Title: {parent title}

Description: {parent description}

{polarity-specific instruction, if applicable}

{feedback on rejected child candidates, only in an additional proposal
round}

Generate between {min_candidate_count} and {max_candidate_count} atomic
completion-point candidates. Do not request, use, or describe any
rollout response texts or per-response judgments. If aggregate feedback
on rejected candidates is supplied, use it only to propose different,
parent-faithful completion points.

For every candidate:

\- Stay inside the exact objective and direction of the parent rubric.

\- Express exactly one objective, factually defensible, query-relevant
detail that a stronger answer should include to complete the parent
requirement.

\- The point may operationalize or add detail to the parent, but must
not introduce a different evaluation objective.

\- Prefer distinct refinement operators when appropriate, such as
mechanism, evidence, boundary condition, consequence, management
implication, operationalization, or a concrete example.

\- Keep the requirement atomic and binary-judgeable from the query and
one answer.

\- Do not add vague demands such as being more comprehensive, detailed,
clear, or accurate.

\- Do not introduce unrelated topics, style preferences, response IDs,
weights, polarity labels, scoring rules, or references to the parent.

\- Make the candidates semantically distinct, not paraphrases of one
another or of candidates identified as rejected in the additional-round
feedback.

\- Match the language of the parent rubric.

Return only a short standalone title and the single completion_point for
each candidate.

The proposal model outputs a JSON candidates array whose entries contain
title and completion_point. In the main configuration, up to five
initial candidates are considered per parent. Candidate children are
judged on the current rollout group and filtered for reward
discrimination. When the number of eligible children is below the
required minimum, an additional proposal round (at most one) is
triggered. The second round uses the same query and parent requirement,
augmented with feedback identifying rejected child proposals and their
aggregate judgment outcomes; no rollout responses are shown to the
proposal model. New candidates are judged and filtered using the same
criterion. Up to three eligible children are retained per parent,
subject to a maximum of three active children per query. If no eligible
child is retained, the original parent contribution is preserved.

### E.3 Rubric Evaluation Prompt

The binary rubric judge evaluates a single public final answer against
the query and numbered rubric descriptions, without observing reference
answers, other responses, rubric weights, hidden reasoning, or training
statistics. When applicable, the public answer is extracted after
\</think\>. If no usable final answer can be extracted, all rubric
verdicts are recorded as NOT_PRESENT. Rubric weights are applied only
during downstream reward aggregation.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Given a user prompt, a generated response, and a list of quality
rubrics, evaluate the response against EACH rubric.

For each rubric:

\- Mark "PRESENT" if the criterion is satisfied, or "NOT_PRESENT" if it
is not. For example, given the response "Apples are red", the rubric
"Mentions apples" is PRESENT, "Does not mention strawberries" is also
PRESENT since the response does not mention strawberries, and "Mentions
oranges" is NOT_PRESENT. Likewise, "Avoids mentioning strawberries" is
PRESENT, while "Avoids mentioning apples" is NOT_PRESENT.

\- If a rubric contains multiple sentences or criteria, consider all of
them. If any required part is not met, mark it NOT_PRESENT. Return
PRESENT only if the entire rubric is met.

\- When a rubric gives examples with wording such as "such as", "for
example", or "including", the response does not need to include every
example. Satisfying one valid listed example can satisfy the criterion.
There is no partial credit.

Return only one strict JSON object. Its keys must be the rubric numbers
and its values must be exactly "PRESENT" or "NOT_PRESENT". Do not return
Markdown, reasons, or extra keys.

The output object must contain exactly one key for each numbered rubric,
with no omissions or extras. For two rubrics, a valid example is:
{"1":"PRESENT","2":"NOT_PRESENT"}. Verify the key count before
responding.

\<Prompt\>

{query}

\</Prompt\>

\<Response\>

{one public final answer}

\</Response\>

\<Rubrics\>

1. {rubric description}

2. {rubric description}

…

\</Rubrics\>

For post-training evaluation, we apply the same per-rubric binary
judgment instructions and strict JSON output format to frozen model
responses, substituting the evaluation query and response for the
training inputs. Training-time rubric judgments are provided by
Qwen3-32B; benchmark evaluation uses the judges specified in
Appendix [A.5](#A1.SS5 "A.5 Evaluation and Judges ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Settings ‣ RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers").
````
